outline.chapter_title: Case Background, Procedural Posture, and Standards of Review
outline.description: This chapter introduces the patents-in-suit, the underlying technology regarding intermodulation product interference, the parties, the procedural history from trial through appeal, and the legal standards governing the Federal Circuit's review of the district court's decisions.
subtopics: The technology: intermodulation products (IMPs), passive intermodulation products (PIM), and PIM cancellation in radios
The '134 and '775 patents: general subject matter and asserted claims
Parties, infringement allegations against AT&T using Nokia radios, and Nokia's intervention
Trial proceedings: jury verdict of validity and infringement, and $166,303,391 lump-sum damages award
Post-trial motions: JMOL of noninfringement, JMOL on damages, and new trial—all denied by the district court
Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1)

Standards of review: JMOL under Fifth Circuit law (de novo, with the 'reasonable juror' standard), substantial evidence for jury infringement findings, claim construction (de novo with clear error review of underlying factual findings), and denial of new trial (abuse of discretion)

outline.chapter_title: The '134 Patent: Infringement Theory and the Insufficiency of Self-Contradictory Expert Testimony
outline.description: This chapter examines the '134 patent's representative claim and key limitations, Finesse's infringement theory based on Dr. Wells' expert testimony, the fundamental flaw in that theory regarding signal generation timing, Dr. Wells' contradictory attempts to pivot his theory, and the Federal Circuit's conclusion that self-contradictory expert testimony cannot support a jury verdict as a matter of law.
subtopics: The '134 patent claims: isolating 'signals of interest' from 'interference generating signals,' computing IMP estimates, and performing closed-loop phase and amplitude adjustment
Key limitation 1[a]: the requirement that the receiver over-sample a passband of received signals including both 'signals of interest' and 'interference generating signals'
Dr. Wells' initial infringement theory: mapping the DL(TX) reference to 'signals of interest' and the modeled PIM path to 'interference generating signals,' both on the red path entering the RF ADC
The fundamental flaw: the modeled PIM path is generated downstream of the RF ADC in the GROOT FPGA, after sampling occurs—signals cannot be sampled before they are generated
Dr. Wells' contradictory pivot: referencing x1 and x2 without ever mapping them onto the claimed 'signals of interest' and 'interference generating signals'
The district court's erroneous finding that Dr. Wells 'clearly' referred to x1 and x2 as the claimed signals
Finesse's argument on appeal that Dr. Wells was 'laboring under a misimpression' and the Federal Circuit's rejection of piecing together fragments of testimony ninety pages apart
Application of Johns Hopkins Univ. v. Datascope Corp.: a party bearing the burden of proof cannot sustain a verdict on an expert's self-contradictory testimony
Reversal of JMOL denial: the jury's infringement verdict for the '134 patent was not supported by substantial evidence

outline.chapter_title: The '775 Patent: Claim Construction and Prosecution History
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the '775 patent's claims requiring seven multiplications of three signals, the district court's claim construction of 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' as 'separately identifiable' but not 'unique,' and the prosecution history argument regarding surrender of claim scope that the Federal Circuit rejected.
subtopics: The '775 patent claims: generating IMP cancellation signals by digitally multiplying three signals (S1, S2, S3) in seven specific third-order multiplications

The district court's claim construction: 'three signals S1, S2 and S3' construed as 'separately identifiable' but not 'unique,' supported by intrinsic and extrinsic evidence including inventor testimony

Appellants' prosecution history argument: Finesse amended claims from 'two or three signals' to 'three signals' to overcome the Filipovic prior art reference, thereby surrendering claim scope over products using only two signals
The Federal Circuit's rejection: Finesse overcame the rejection primarily by distinguishing Filipovic as limited to active IMPs, not passive IMPs

Application of Continental Circuits LLC v. Intel Corp.: the amendment to 'three signals' does not constitute a 'clear and unambiguous' disavowal of claim scope over products with two unique input signals
The distinction between three 'separately identifiable' signals and three 'unique' input signals, and why two signals plus a copy of one may satisfy the claim construction

outline.chapter_title: The '775 Patent: Substantial Evidence of the Seven Claimed Multiplications
outline.description: This chapter examines Finesse's infringement evidence regarding the seven claimed multiplications, the shortcomings of Dr. Wells' testimony, Finesse's flawed mapping attempts at trial and on appeal, and the Federal Circuit's conclusion that no reasonable jury could find the accused radios perform all seven claimed multiplications.
subtopics: Dr. Wells' reliance on Nokia technical documents to show the accused radios perform the claimed multiplications
The three distinct multiplications identified in the Nokia document: x1⋅|x1|⋅|x1|, x1⋅x1⋅x2', and x1⋅|x2|⋅|x2|—using modulus and complex conjugate operations, not simple signal multiplication
Dr. Wells' failure to testify how the three distinct multiplications map onto the seven claimed multiplications in limitation 1[d]
The district court's reasoning: three distinct multiplications are sufficient because each corresponds to two or three of the seven claimed multiplications

Finesse's flawed mapping on appeal: requiring S3 to simultaneously map onto the signal x2, its complex conjugate x2', and its modulus |x2|, which contradicts the claim construction of separately identifiable signals
Finesse's 'ten multiplications' argument at oral argument and the absence of any explanation mapping a subset of ten to the seven claimed multiplications
Evidence never presented to the jury cannot support the verdict, and no reasonable jury could find infringement based on the evidence at trial
Reversal of JMOL denial: the jury's infringement verdict for the '775 patent was not supported by substantial evidence

outline.description: This chapter addresses the jury's damages award, the district court's denial of JMOL and new trial on damages, and the Federal Circuit's vacatur of the damages award as a necessary consequence of reversing the infringement verdict for all asserted claims of both patents.
subtopics: The jury's $166,303,391 lump-sum damages award for the remaining life of the '134 and '775 patents
Appellants' post-trial motions for JMOL on damages and, in the alternative, a new trial on damages
The district court's denial of both damages motions
The Federal Circuit's vacatur of the damages award as a consequence of reversing JMOL of noninfringement for all asserted claims of both patents
Final disposition: reversal of the denial of JMOL of noninfringement and vacatur of the damages award, with costs to Appellants
